query: For a CoCrFeNi high-entropy-alloy matrix evaluated in sliding from room temperature to 800 °C, what single intervention could overcome the difficulty of maintaining low coefficient of friction and wear rate throughout the full temperature range? Earlier studies of other self-lubricating material systems reported low coefficients of friction at 704 °C and favorable friction and wear behavior over broad temperature ranges. However, these results do not resolve the limited understanding of wide-temperature tribological performance in CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloys, and effectiveness must be maintained as operating temperature, load, and environment vary. Formulate one hypothesis that identifies a single intervention without presupposing its class, explains its mechanism, predicts friction and wear relative to the starting CoCrFeNi material, defines its temperature, load, and environmental boundaries, relates it to prior evidence, and specifies a controlled experiment with a clear result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Introducing a minor, carefully controlled dopant element into the CoCrFeNi matrix will promote the in‐situ formation of a self-adaptive, lubricious glaze layer during sliding that is maintained over the full temperature range (room temperature to 800 °C), thereby reducing both friction and wear consistently across variable loads and environmental conditions.
generation.material_initial_state: A conventionally processed, single-phase, coarse-grained CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloy that exhibits dynamic shear-induced grain refinement under sliding but suffers from variable tribological performance as temperature and load change.
generation.intervention: Incorporate a small amount of a reactive dopant (without predefining its chemical class) designed to segregate to the surface under sliding conditions so as to trigger controlled oxidation and extreme grain refinement. This dopant aids the formation of a protective nano-grained glaze layer during sliding.
generation.conditions: Tribological tests performed under sliding contact in ambient conditions with controlled oxygen availability, across a temperature range from room temperature to 800 °C, and under varied normal loads and sliding speeds.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of a continuous, nano-grained surface glaze integrating beneficial oxide phases and nanoprecipitates that stabilize the interface, thereby mediating shear deformation and reducing friction.
generation.mechanism: Upon sliding, the dopant migrates to the wear interface where it promotes controlled oxidation and enhances dynamic grain refinement. This results in an adaptive glaze layer that exhibits inverse Hall-Petch behavior (softening due to extreme grain refinement) at lower temperatures and forms a robust, protective oxide film at higher temperatures. Together, these changes lower shear strength and inhibit adhesive, oxidative, and plastic deformation wear mechanisms.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the undoped CoCrFeNi alloy, the doped alloy will achieve a lower coefficient of friction (approaching values near 0.2) and markedly reduced wear rates (by one to several orders of magnitude improvement) across the full span of temperatures and under both high and low load conditions. The beneficial effect will be most apparent in maintaining stable tribological behavior despite thermal and mechanical stresses.
generation.baseline: The baseline performance is defined by the existing CoCrFeNi alloy's behavior, which, while showing evidence of dynamic shear-induced grain refinement, exhibits inconsistent friction and wear characteristics over the temperature range due to unstable oxide formation and insufficient interface adaptation.
generation.boundary: This intervention is expected to be effective in ambient (oxidizing) environments up to 800 °C and under the range of sliding loads typically used in tribological testing. Its benefits in inert or ultrahigh vacuum environments, or under extreme load beyond tested ranges, remain uncertain.
generation.uncertainty: The optimal dopant choice and concentration, and the precise balance between promoting grain refinement and generating a protective oxide layer without inducing embrittlement or adverse phase transformations, remain to be experimentally determined. Additionally, the interplay between dynamic mechanical conditions and chemical effects may vary with environmental factors.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of CoCrFeNi alloy samples: one set with the controlled dopant addition and one undoped set as the baseline. Conduct ball-on-disk sliding tests over the temperature range of room temperature to 800 °C under identical, well-controlled loads and ambient conditions. Use high-resolution microscopy to characterize the wear tracks and analyze the surface for evidence of a continuous glaze layer as well as grain size refinements.
measurements: Coefficient of friction (μ) during steady-state sliding
Surface microstructure (grain size, presence of oxide phases, and glaze continuity) via SEM/TEM
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the doped samples do not show a statistically significant reduction in friction (targeting ~0.2) and wear rate across the entire temperature range compared to the undoped baseline, or if microstructural analysis does not reveal the formation of a continuous and adaptive lubricious glaze layer, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: AbstractSustained wear damages on the sliding surfaces of alloys are generally the culprit responsible for the failure of various mechanical systems. Inspired by high-entropy effects, here we deliberately deploy nanohierarchical architecture with composition undulation in a Ni50(AlNbTiV)50 complex concentrated alloy, which yields ultralow wear rate within the order of 10−7 to 10−6 mm3/Nm between room temperature and 800 °C. Such remarkable wear resistance heretofore represents one of the highest wear resistance reported for the bulk alloys or composites, and originates from the multi-type adaptive friction interface protection governed by intrinsically nano-coupled grains and nanoprecipitates. This cooperative heterostructure releases gradient frictional stress in stages upon wear at room temperature through the coexistence of multiple deformation pathways while activating a dense nanocrystalline glaze layer upon wear at 800 °C to minimize adhesive and oxidative wear. Our work uncovers a practical avenue for tailoring wear properties with multicomponent heterostructures over a wide temperature range.

AbstractThe effect and mechanism of grain sizes on the tribological behavior of CoCrFeMnNi high entropy alloy (HEA) were studied by friction experiments and wear morphology analysis. Under normal low load and low sliding speed, the primary wear mechanism of the HEA samples is adhesive wear. With the increase in sliding speed, the wear mechanisms of the samples are adhesive wear and oxidation wear. The oxide layer formed under the action of friction heat of the coarse grain (CG) sample is easy to break due to the softening of the CG. With the increase of normal load and sliding speed, the wear mechanisms of the HEA samples are mainly adhesive wear, oxidation wear, and plastic deformation. The oxide layer of CG sample has many cracks, and the worn surface also has plastic deformation, which leads to the increase of friction coefficient and specific wear rate and the decrease of wear resistance. Therefore, the fine grain size HEA sample has better wear resistance than the CG sample due to its high surface strength.Keywords: high entropy alloy, grain size, tribological behavior, wear mechanism
